source: KDT8 ch1, KDT8 ch3; GG14 ch2; RangDale9 ch9

cards.front: What are the advantages of making a drug long-acting?
cards.back: Fewer doses and better compliance (a single daily dose or a monthly/quarterly contraceptive is less often missed); smoother plasma levels, so peak-related side effects (e.g. nifedipine) fall and troughs are avoided; and the effect lasts overnight without waking the patient (antiasthmatics, anticonvulsants).

cards.front: Which drugs are suitable, and which unsuitable, for controlled-release formulations?
cards.back: Suitable: drugs with short half-lives (under 4 h), and selected groups such as patients on antiepileptics or antipsychotics. Not needed: drugs with half-life above 12 h or inherently long action (doxycycline, omeprazole, digoxin, amlodipine), and drugs wanted only briefly (hypnotics, headache remedies).

cards.front: Classify: methods of prolonging drug action
cards.text: 1. Prolonging {{absorption}}: oral sustained/controlled release, parenteral depot or implants, {{transdermal}} systems. 2. Increasing {{plasma protein binding}} (sulfadoxine). 3. Retarding {{metabolism}} (ethinyl estradiol; ritonavir boosting protease inhibitors; cilastatin protecting imipenem; allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine). 4. Retarding {{renal excretion}} (probenecid with penicillin).

cards.front: Short note: Chronopharmacology and timing of drug therapy

points: Chronopharmacology studies how daily biological rhythms change drug action
The same dose can act differently depending on the time of day it is given
Cortisol secretion follows a circadian rhythm, peaking in early morning
Tissue sensitivity to glucocorticoids runs opposite to cortisol: highest in evening and early night
A single morning corticosteroid dose causes less pituitary-adrenal suppression
Hypnotics work more easily when taken at night in quiet surroundings
Statins inhibit cholesterol synthesis more when taken in the late evening
Timing relative to meals also changes absorption of some drugs
Choose the dosing time to limit side effects such as adrenal suppression
Timed-release forms can copy the natural daily pattern, as timed hydrocortisone tablets do in replacement therapy

cards.front: Probenecid with penicillin, cilastatin with imipenem, allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine: what do they share, and how does each prolong action?
cards.back: Each partner slows the elimination of the first drug. Probenecid retards renal excretion of penicillin; cilastatin protects imipenem and allopurinol protects 6-mercaptopurine by retarding metabolism. Contrast: sulfadoxine is long-acting through high plasma protein binding, and ethinyl estradiol through slow metabolism.

cards.front: Essay: Novel drug delivery systems

points: Reduce dosing frequency and improve compliance
Smooth plasma levels; fewer peak-related effects
Localise drug to target and spare other tissues
Sustained/extended release tablets, spansules
Controlled release through semipermeable membrane
Enteric coating
Insoluble salts and suspensions (benzathine penicillin, lente insulin)
Oily esters (fluphenazine decanoate, depot progestins)
Pellets and silastic or biodegradable implants
TTS: GTN, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol
Nasal sprays for peptides; eye drops
Inhaled aerosols for lung
Liposomes (amphotericin B, doxorubicin)
Antibody-drug conjugates
Nanoparticles (albumin-bound paclitaxel)
Prodrugs; GalNAc-tagged nucleic acid drugs to liver
Drug-eluting stents (sirolimus)
Progestin-releasing IUCD
Microneedle patches

cards.front: Differentiate sustained-release from controlled-release oral tablets.
cards.back: Sustained/extended release: drug particles coated with resins, plastics or other materials that dissolve at different rates, spreading release over time. Controlled release: a semipermeable membrane governs release; in the KDT example about 30% of the dose outside the membrane is released at once and 70% over the next 4-8 hours.

cards.front: What are spansules and enteric-coated capsules?
cards.back: Spansules are extended-release capsules filled with drug granules carrying different coatings that dissolve over a range of times. Enteric-coated capsules dissolve only on reaching the ileum; enteric-coated tablets resist gastric acid and break up in the duodenum.

cards.front: Which problems of oral therapy do enteric-coated and sustained-release preparations overcome?
cards.back: Acid lability (e.g. destruction by gastric acid), gastric irritancy and a short duration of action.

cards.front: What are the parts of an osmotic pump oral tablet?
cards.back: A core holding the drug and an osmogen, a semipermeable membrane coat, and a delivery orifice made by laser or mechanical drilling.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Osmotic Pump Drug Delivery Systems: A Comprehensive Review (Almoshari, Pharmaceuticals 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9697821/

cards.front: What is the role of the osmogen in an osmotic pump?
cards.back: It creates the osmotic gradient that draws water in. It also speeds release of poorly soluble drugs.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Osmotic Pump Drug Delivery Systems: A Comprehensive Review (Almoshari, Pharmaceuticals 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9697821/

cards.front: How does the volume of drug released relate to water entry in an osmotic pump?
cards.back: It is proportional to the volume of water that enters the core.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Osmotic Pump Drug Delivery Systems: A Comprehensive Review (Almoshari, Pharmaceuticals 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9697821/

cards.front: What are the limitations of oral sustained- or controlled-release preparations?
cards.back: They prolong action by only about 4-8 hours, because by then the particles reach the colon; and drug release, and so blood levels, can be more variable than with a regular tablet of the same drug.

cards.front: Why do modified-release preparations matter in overdose?
cards.back: Sustained, controlled or extended release forms change the time to peak concentration, so absorption is delayed and prolonged and toxicity may appear late or last longer.

cards.front: How does a controlled-release tablet with a semipermeable membrane release its drug?
cards.back: About 30% of the dose, outside the membrane, is released at once, and the remaining 70% is released slowly through the membrane over the next 4 to 8 hours. Such preparations prolong action by 4 to 8 hours and no longer.

cards.front: How does an osmotic pump push drug out?
cards.back: Water passes through the membrane into the core, raising osmotic pressure, which pushes drug solution out through the orifice.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Osmotic Pump Drug Delivery Systems: A Comprehensive Review (Almoshari, Pharmaceuticals 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9697821/

cards.front: What release pattern does an osmotic pump give?
cards.back: Zero-order release after a lag of about 30 to 60 minutes; about 60 to 80% of the drug is released at this constant rate.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Osmotic Pump Drug Delivery Systems: A Comprehensive Review (Almoshari, Pharmaceuticals 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9697821/

cards.front: Floating gastroretentive form: density and how it floats?
cards.back: Density below that of gastric contents (about 1.004 g/mL). Effervescent types generate CO2; non-effervescent types rely on swelling hydrocolloids.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: Swelling-type (plug) gastroretentive system: how is it retained?
cards.back: It expands in gastric fluid to a size larger than the pyloric opening. Swelling depends on the cross-linking of the polymer network.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: High-density gastroretentive system: how is it retained?
cards.back: It is heavier than gastric contents and sinks to the bottom of the stomach. The article cites an ideal density of 1.0 to 2.5 g/cm3.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: Short note: Gastroretentive drug delivery systems

points: Keep the dosage form in gastric fluid so the drug releases in the stomach
Narrow absorption window
Unstable at alkaline pH
Dissolve better at low pH
Absorbed mainly from the stomach
Floating (low density, below gastric contents)
Swelling (plug type, larger than the pyloric opening)
Mucoadhesive
High density (sinks to the stomach bottom)

refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: A drug has a half-life of 3 h and is absorbed mainly from the stomach. Justify the choice among a sustained-release tablet, an osmotic pump tablet and a gastroretentive form.
cards.back: Half-life under 4 h makes it a fit for modified release. An ordinary sustained-release tablet prolongs action only 4-8 h and is variable, because particles reach the colon before release ends. A narrow, stomach-based absorption window argues for a gastroretentive system (floating, swelling or high density) that keeps the dose in gastric fluid. An osmotic pump gives steady zero-order release and suits drugs whose absorption site is not limiting.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Osmotic Pump Drug Delivery Systems: A Comprehensive Review (Almoshari, Pharmaceuticals 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9697821/
WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: Give examples of depot injections that delay absorption.
cards.back: Insoluble forms: benzathine or procaine penicillin, lente insulin (insulin with protamine and zinc). Oily solutions of esters: depot progestins (medroxyprogesterone acetate), testosterone propionate, fluphenazine decanoate. A vasoconstrictor such as adrenaline with a local anaesthetic also delays absorption.

cards.front: What are pellet implants and silastic/biodegradable implants?
cards.back: Pellet: a solid drug pellet inserted subcutaneously with a trocar and cannula, releasing drug over weeks to months (DOCA, testosterone, oestradiol); absorption rate is proportional to the implant surface area. Silastic (non-biodegradable) or biodegradable implants: crystalline drug in tubes or capsules under the skin that leach evenly for months (hormones, contraceptives such as Norplant); the non-biodegradable kind must later be removed.

cards.front: What is a dermojet?
cards.back: A needle-free gun that fires a high-velocity jet of drug solution through a tiny orifice; the drug passes through the superficial skin and is deposited subcutaneously. It is nearly painless and suits mass inoculation.

cards.front: What is Norplant, and how long does it provide contraception?
cards.back: A subcutaneous implant of six capsules, each containing 36 mg levonorgestrel. It provides contraception for up to 5 years.

cards.front: How is the rate of subcutaneous insulin absorption deliberately varied?
cards.back: By changing particle size, complexing with protein, and adjusting pH of the preparation.

cards.front: What does continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion by pump offer compared with injections?
cards.back: A constant basal insulin infusion with programmed meal boluses, using short-acting insulin only. Insulin is otherwise given as subcutaneous injections by syringe or prefilled pen.

cards.front: How does a prodrug approach prolong action for a drug with a short half-life?
cards.back: Long-chain aliphatic esters are used because they hydrolyse slowly. When injected, such a prodrug can act for about a month. Bitolterol-O-di-p-toluate is an example. The slow release means the drug does not need frequent dosing.

cards.front: Short note: Newer drug delivery systems of insulin

points: Absorption rate is varied by particle size, protein complexation and pH of the preparation
Insulin is made insoluble either by complexing with protamine (isophane/NPH) or by precipitating with excess zinc (lente, larger particles), so it is absorbed slowly
Continuous subcutaneous infusion gives constant basal insulin plus programmed meal boluses
Only short-acting insulin is used in the pump
Otherwise insulin is given by syringe or prefilled pen injections

cards.front: Compare oily-ester depot injections, pellet implants and silastic implants as ways to prolong action.
cards.back: All delay absorption at the injection or implant site. Oily esters and insoluble salts (fluphenazine decanoate, medroxyprogesterone, benzathine penicillin) release over days to weeks. A pellet gives weeks to months, its rate proportional to surface area, and is placed with a trocar. Silastic tubes or capsules (Norplant: six capsules of levonorgestrel, up to 5 years) leach evenly for months; non-biodegradable ones must be removed later, biodegradable ones need not.

cards.front: Which body sites are used for transdermal patches, and what factors govern skin absorption?
cards.back: Chest, abdomen, upper arm, lower back, buttock or mastoid region (KDT). Absorption depends on the area covered and the drug's lipid solubility; it is much greater through abraded, burned or denuded skin, and is increased by an oily vehicle with rubbing and by hydrating the skin.

cards.front: Describe the layers of a transdermal therapeutic system.
cards.back: An adhesive patch of 5 to 20 cm2. The drug, in solution or bound to a polymer, sits in a reservoir between an occlusive backing film and a rate-controlling micropore membrane. The skin-side adhesive carries a priming dose and is covered by a peel-off film. Systems are designed to last 1 to 3 days and give smooth plasma levels.

cards.front: Name three drugs given by transdermal patch and their indications.
cards.back: Nicotine for smoking withdrawal; a nitrate (glyceryl trinitrate) for chronic angina; scopolamine (hyoscine) for motion sickness.

cards.front: Which inhaler types are used for bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids?
cards.back: Ipratropium is given up to four times daily by metered-dose inhaler or nebuliser. Tiotropium and aclidinium are given as dry powder inhalers. Inhaled corticosteroids are given by metered-dose or dry-powder inhaler.

cards.front: How does mucoadhesion hold a dosage form in place?
cards.back: By hydration, bonding or receptor interactions with the mucosa, keeping the drug at one site for an extended period.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: Name polymers used in mucoadhesive systems.
cards.back: Natural: sodium alginate, gelatin, guar gum. Semisynthetic: HPMC, carbopol, sodium carboxymethyl cellulose.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Features and Facts of a Gastroretentive Drug Delivery System: A Review (Turk J Pharm Sci 2022) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9438753/

cards.front: Short note: Transdermal therapeutic systems

points: Occlusive backing film
Drug reservoir (solution or polymer-bound)
Rate-controlling micropore membrane
Adhesive layer with priming dose; peel-off liner
Membrane delivers drug more slowly than the slowest skin absorption, so rate is constant at any site
Suits only lipid-soluble drugs (Rang & Dale)
GTN, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol (India)
Isosorbide dinitrate, hyoscine, clonidine (elsewhere)
Testosterone patches
Smooth plasma level; little first-pass metabolism
Less inter-individual variation and fewer side effects
Better compliance; lasts 1-3 days
Cost
Local irritation and erythema: rotate sites

cards.front: Which drugs are given as nasal sprays, and why does this route work for peptides?
cards.back: Peptide hormone analogues such as antidiuretic hormone and GnRH analogues, and calcitonin. Absorption is thought to occur through the unusually permeable mucosa over nasal-associated lymphoid tissue, similar to that over Peyer's patches.

cards.front: How do inhaled and ocular delivery achieve local action, and what are their limits?
cards.back: Inhaled glucocorticoids (beclometasone) and bronchodilators give high lung levels with little systemic exposure; ipratropium, a quaternary analogue of atropine, is poorly absorbed, which further limits systemic effects. Eye drops such as dorzolamide lower intraocular pressure without the acidosis of oral acetazolamide. Some systemic absorption still occurs: tremor with salbutamol, bronchospasm with timolol eye drops.

cards.front: On what does the dose from a transdermal patch depend, and does the skin site matter?
cards.back: The dose depends on the patch area: 10, 20 and 30 cm2 nicotine patches release 7, 14 and 21 mg per 24 hours. A transdermal system releases at a constant rate whatever the skin site, because its membrane sets the rate.

cards.front: How does inhaled particle size affect where an aerosol deposits?
cards.back: Aerosol particles of about 2 to 5 micrometres mostly deposit in the mouth or pharynx (80 to 90% of the dose). Particles under 1 to 2 micrometres stay suspended and may be exhaled. Gases and volatile anaesthetics act systemically after absorption from the alveoli.

cards.front: Why are nicotine, nitroglycerin and hyoscine given by patch, whereas ADH and GnRH analogues are given nasally?
cards.back: Patches need lipid-soluble drugs and a rate-controlling membrane, giving constant, smooth delivery at any site for 1-3 days (smoking withdrawal, chronic angina, motion sickness). Peptides such as ADH and GnRH analogues are given nasally because the mucosa over nasal-associated lymphoid tissue is unusually permeable.

cards.front: What are antibody-drug conjugates? Name two approved examples.
cards.back: A cytotoxic drug or toxin attached to an antibody against a tumour antigen, so it binds tumour cells selectively. Examples: ado-trastuzumab emtansine (metastatic breast cancer) and brentuximab vedotin (Hodgkin lymphoma).

cards.front: What newer delivery approaches does GG14 list?
cards.back: Drug-eluting stents, microneedle patches, biocompatible polymers and nanoparticles, used to target drugs locally and cut systemic exposure. Albumin-nanoparticle paclitaxel for breast cancer is an approved nanoparticle example (Rang & Dale).

cards.front: Classify: special drug delivery systems (Rang & Dale)
cards.text: Approaches to localise drugs include {{prodrugs}}, {{antibody-drug conjugates}}, packaging in {{liposomes}} and {{coated implantable devices}}.

cards.front: Short note: Liposomes as drug carriers

points: Phospholipid vesicles made by sonication (lecithin or other biodegradable lipids)
KDT: uni- or bilamellar nanovesicles; Rang & Dale: 0.1-1 micrometre
Carry non-lipid-soluble drug until disrupted
Taken up by reticuloendothelial cells of liver and spleen
Concentrate in some malignant tumours
Antibody tagging under trial for other tissues
Liposomal amphotericin B: kala-azar and systemic mycoses; less nephrotoxic but costly
Liposomal doxorubicin: ovarian cancer, myeloma
Liposomal cytarabine (intrathecal) and vincristine

cards.front: Give examples of prodrugs used as a delivery strategy.
cards.back: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the liver, sparing the gut epithelium when taken orally. Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier on an amino acid carrier before conversion to dopamine. Valaciclovir and famciclovir are ester prodrugs with better bioavailability than aciclovir and penciclovir. Zidovudine is activated only in HIV-infected cells. Aspirin was made as a better-tolerated form of salicylic acid.

cards.front: How are nucleic acid drugs (siRNA, antisense) delivered selectively to hepatocytes?
cards.back: They are linked to galactose or N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), which binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor abundant on hepatocytes, leading to selective uptake. Early studies show benefit in dyslipidaemia, haemophilia and a form of amyloidosis.

cards.front: Short note: Liposomes for targeted drug delivery

points: Unilamellar or bilamellar nano-vesicles made by sonicating lecithin or other biodegradable phospholipids
Lipid vesicles carry drugs, which can be targeted to specific tissues (KDT8 section on routes and delivery)

cards.front: What is the role of nanoparticles in drug delivery, and what examples are given?
cards.back: Biocompatible polymers and nanoparticles are carriers that localise drug to a target and cut systemic exposure. Example: albumin-nanoparticle paclitaxel for breast cancer. Related targeting uses GalNAc conjugates to carry siRNA to hepatocytes via the asialoglycoprotein receptor.

cards.front: Short note: Targeted drug delivery in cancer therapy

points: Improve selectivity of cytotoxic drugs so they reach tumour cells
Limit damage to normal tissue
Cytotoxic drug or toxin linked to an antibody against a tumour-specific antigen
Ado-trastuzumab emtansine: metastatic breast cancer; brentuximab vedotin: Hodgkin's lymphoma
Vesicles of about 0.1 to 1 micrometre; carry non-lipid-soluble drugs
Concentrate in malignant tumours; taken up by reticuloendothelial cells, mainly in liver
Several liposomal chemotherapy formulations are available
Cyclophosphamide is active only after hepatic activation, so it can be given orally
Nanoparticles and biocompatible polymers are recent advances in delivery

cards.front: Short note: Prodrugs and their clinical implications

points: Inactive precursor converted in the body to the active drug
Used to localise action, improve bioavailability or tolerability
Cyclophosphamide: activated in liver, can be given orally without gut damage
Levodopa: crosses blood-brain barrier on an amino acid carrier, then becomes dopamine
Valaciclovir, famciclovir: esters with better bioavailability than aciclovir and penciclovir
Zidovudine: activated only in HIV-infected cells
Aspirin: better-tolerated form of salicylic acid
Long-chain aliphatic esters hydrolyse slowly; one injection can act about a month (bitolterol-O-di-p-toluate)

cards.front: Essay: Targeted drug delivery systems

points: Aim: drug concentrated at the target, less systemic exposure
Prodrugs (cyclophosphamide, levodopa, valaciclovir)
Antibody-drug conjugates (ado-trastuzumab emtansine, brentuximab vedotin)
Liposomes (nano-sized phospholipid vesicles; amphotericin B, doxorubicin)
Nanoparticles (albumin-bound paclitaxel)
GalNAc-linked nucleic acids to hepatocytes via ASGR
Drug-eluting stents (sirolimus), hormone-releasing IUDs, ocular inserts
Selectivity comes from a target-specific ligand (antibody, receptor sugar) or an activation step confined to the target

cards.front: What are drug-eluting stents, and why are they used?
cards.back: Stents placed in a coronary artery after balloon angioplasty, coated with antithrombotic or antiproliferative drug (e.g. sirolimus in a surface polymer). They reduce restenosis and angioplasty failure, though restenosis can still occur at the stent margin.

cards.front: Give examples of drug-releasing implants for local hormonal delivery.
cards.back: Progestin-impregnated intrauterine devices release hormone to the endometrium, giving contraceptive protection for up to 5 years (KDT); implanted or oral controlled-release devices also provide long-acting contraception (GG14).

cards.front: What is Ocusert, and what do GG14 say about ocular inserts?
cards.back: Ocusert is a drug-filled polymer insert placed in the lower conjunctival sac. It releases pilocarpine at a controlled rate. GG14 notes that drug-loaded contact lenses and ocular inserts place drugs where they are needed.

cards.front: Why does coating a coronary stent with a drug reduce angioplasty failure, and what limit remains?
cards.back: After balloon angioplasty the artery tends to narrow again (restenosis). An antiproliferative or antithrombotic drug (e.g. sirolimus in a surface polymer) acts locally at the stent, so effect is concentrated where needed. Restenosis can still occur at the stent margin.

cards.front: Compare progestin IUD, Norplant implant and Ocusert as drug-releasing devices.
cards.back: All release drug at a controlled rate. The IUD releases hormone to the endometrium, protecting up to 5 years. Norplant (subcutaneous, six capsules) also lasts up to 5 years. Ocusert sits in the lower conjunctival sac and releases pilocarpine in the eye.

cards.front: Short note: Drug-releasing devices (stents, IUDs, inserts)

points: Device carries drug and releases it at the site, sparing other tissues
Drug-eluting coronary stent: sirolimus or antithrombotic coat, less restenosis
Progestin IUD: endometrial delivery, up to 5 years
Ocusert: pilocarpine in lower conjunctival sac
GG14: contact lenses, microneedle patches, polymers
Restenosis can still occur at stent margin

cards.front: Essay: Inhaled medicines: current and future perspectives

points: Inhalation delivers drug straight to the airways for local action
Gases and volatile liquids are inhaled; non-volatile liquids and fine solids are aerosolised
Optimum 2–5 µm MMAD settles in the airways
Larger particles stop in the upper airway; smaller ones are exhaled
About 1 µm particles are of growing interest, now possible with HFA
pMDI with HFA propellant (CFC propellants replaced)
Spacer chamber reduces oropharyngeal deposition
DPI needs a minimum inspiratory flow; hard for children under 7
Nebulisers (jet or ultrasonic): higher doses during tidal breathing
Only 10–20% of a pMDI dose reaches the lower airways
The rest is swallowed: systemic exposure and first-pass metabolism
Oral dose is about 20 times the inhaled dose for the same pulmonary effect
Inhaled route preferred when the patient can use it
Inhaled corticosteroids and β2 agonists in asthma and COPD
Antimuscarinics such as ipratropium; tiotropium once daily
Salbutamol (SABA) is used as required for symptom relief
Inhaled HFA steroids reach smaller airways but raise systemic absorption
Insulin by DPI: dosing consistency remains a problem
Inhalation gives local action with less systemic exposure, but device technique and dosing consistency decide outcome

cards.front: What is MMAD, and which particle size settles in the airways?
cards.back: Mass median aerodynamic diameter. 2–5 µm settles in the airways; larger particles stop in the upper airway and smaller ones are exhaled.

cards.front: What is a spacer chamber used with a pMDI?
cards.back: A large-volume chamber between inhaler and mouth. It slows particles and lets propellant evaporate, so less drug hits the oropharynx and more reaches the lower airways.

cards.front: Why does a pMDI put only 10–20% of its dose into the lower airways?
cards.back: Most drug deposits in the mouth and pharynx and is swallowed. It is then absorbed from the gut and undergoes first-pass metabolism. Only the inhaled fraction reaches the lungs.

cards.front: Why is an HFA-formulated inhaled steroid a trade-off for systemic risk?
cards.back: It delivers drug to smaller airways, but more is absorbed into the bronchial circulation. Systemic side effects can rise, so the therapeutic ratio may not improve.

cards.front: Why are nebulisers useful in acute asthma or COPD?
cards.back: They deliver much higher doses than a pMDI during tidal breathing, so they suit acute exacerbations.

cards.front: What limits dry powder inhalers for systemic insulin delivery?
cards.back: Dosing consistency is poor. DPIs also need a minimum inspiratory flow, and children under 7 find them hard to use.

cards.front: Essay: Methods of drug targeting

points: Deliver drug to the target tissue and spare others
Targeting allows larger effective doses without systemic toxicity
Uses vascular differences, e.g. leaky tumour capillaries
High-molecular polymer–drug conjugates accumulate in tumour
Drug released by enzyme cleavage after the carrier enters the cell
Carrier linked to a ligand that cell-surface receptors recognise
Example: antibody to a tumour antigen
Example: galactose to the hepatocyte asialoglycoprotein receptor
Liposomes are taken up by the reticuloendothelial system
PEG (stealth) liposomes circulate for days
Antibody-tagged liposomes (HER2, E-selectin) are under study
Activated in target cells: capecitabine to fluorouracil in tumour; zidovudine in infected cells
Vaginal ring (estradiol), eye implant (ganciclovir), drug-eluting stents, progestin IUCD
Polymers and degradation products must be checked for toxicity
Cost and unwanted rapid release are problems

cards.front: What is passive targeting?
cards.back: Using vascular differences between target and other tissues to deliver drug selectively after IV injection. For example, leaky tumour capillaries let large polymer–drug complexes accumulate.

cards.front: What is active targeting?
cards.back: Linking the carrier to a ligand that cell-surface receptors recognise. Examples: an antibody to a tumour antigen, or galactose for the liver's asialoglycoprotein receptor.

cards.front: How does active targeting differ from passive targeting?
cards.back: Passive targeting depends on tissue vascular features alone. Active targeting adds a receptor-recognised ligand so the carrier binds specific cells.

cards.front: Why do PEG-coated ('stealth') liposomes circulate longer?
cards.back: PEG makes the surface hydrophilic, so less uptake by the reticuloendothelial system. Circulation lasts days, so larger doses can be given.

cards.front: Which antibody targets have been explored for liposomes?
cards.back: HER2 (breast cancer and other tumours) and E-selectin (vascular endothelium).

cards.front: Which prodrug is converted to its active form selectively in tumour cells?
cards.back: Capecitabine, converted to fluorouracil by a tumour-specific enzyme.

cards.front: Give an example of a prodrug activated in virus-infected cells.
cards.back: Zidovudine, which is taken up and activated in infected cells, giving selective toxicity to them.

cards.front: Name two anatomically placed devices for targeted local delivery.
cards.back: Estring (estradiol vaginal ring) and Vitrasert (ganciclovir eye implant).

cards.front: What is a basic limitation of polymer-based delivery systems?
cards.back: Each material and its degradation products must be evaluated for toxic effects.
